Nimble

Game Strategy

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)

Game: slide chips along a row of numbered positions toward zero. You and the computer take turns; whoever moves the last chip to zero wins.
How to play: click a chip to select it, then click any position to its left to move it there. A chip can slide as far as you like in one move.
Look for the math

Nimble looks like a simple sliding game, but it hides a famous game inside it. Once you see the connection, you can beat the computer every time — when the starting position allows it.

Nim in disguise

Each chip's position number is the size of a Nim heap. Moving a chip left reduces its heap. Landing on zero removes the heap. So Nimble with chips at positions 3 and 5 is exactly the same as Nim with heaps of 3 and 5. The game of Sprague–Grundy theory applies directly.

The XOR rule

Write all the chip positions in binary and add them without carrying — that is exclusive or (XOR). When the total is 0, the player whose turn it is will lose if the opponent plays perfectly. When it is not 0, the player to move can always find a move that makes it 0, handing the losing position to the opponent. For a single chip at position p, the Sprague–Grundy value is simply p itself.

How the computer plays

On its turn the computer XORs all the chip positions. If the result is not 0, it finds the chip whose position shares the highest bit with the XOR and moves it to make the total 0. If the XOR is already 0 (the computer is losing), it moves a random chip and hopes you slip. A starting position where all chip positions XOR to 0 is unwinnable for you; otherwise you can always win by moving first to a XOR of 0.

Try one chip on a board of length 7. The chip starts somewhere between 2 and 6 — move it straight to 0 in one jump and you win instantly! With two chips, move one so both positions become equal: equal positions XOR to 0, leaving the computer in a losing spot.
